title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 306: The Invention of the Alphabet
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 306 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Invention of the Alphabet: Script, Statecraft, and Literacy

Paragraph 1. For thousands of years, reading and writing belonged strictly to powerful rulers. In ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, scripts such as cuneiform and hieroglyphics contained hundreds or thousands of picture signs representing entire ideas or royal terms. Mastering these complex systems demanded decades of full-time training, keeping literacy locked inside a small class of priests, royal clerks, and trained scribes. As a result, ordinary workers could not read state laws or business deals without paying an educated expert to read for them.

Paragraph 2. In The Alphabet: A Revolution in Human Thought, historian Dr. Aaron Vance explains how a simpler writing system broke that control. The earliest signs of this phonetic script were not discovered inside rich royal palaces, but inside remote turquoise mines in the Sinai desert. Around 1800 BCE, migrant workers who could not enter elite Egyptian schools adapted roughly two dozen Egyptian picture signs. Instead of drawing whole objects, they used each mark to stand for a single spoken consonant sound.

Paragraph 3. By reducing thousands of complicated symbols to roughly thirty sound letters, the early alphabet saved huge mental effort. Anyone who could speak could learn to read and write within a few weeks instead of decades. Although imperial governments first dismissed this writing as messy graffiti made by slaves and travellers, sea merchants saw its practical power. Phoenician traders quickly adopted the script to record business deals faster, spreading it across sea routes to give birth to Greek, Latin, and most modern alphabets.

Paragraph 4. However, Dr. Vance warns against viewing the alphabet as a purely positive invention without mental costs. He recalls how the Greek philosopher Socrates feared that storing words on paper would weaken natural human memory, giving readers a false sense of wisdom. Vance adds that while ancient picture writing kept a lively visual link to real objects around us, phonetic letters trained human minds toward strict, linear, and abstract thinking.
